🚀 Welcome! I'm Ronald Rivera, CEO of Devebug Industries, Ecuador.

🌎: devebug.com

🌟Our vision goes beyond NASA Space Apps. Promising projects may continue with paid contracts, professional opportunities, and long-term collaboration, subject to funding and viability.
summary: ANALOG-Δ screens Earth for Moon and Mars surface analogs using open NASA data, then tests whether the screening holds up. We compared elevation, slope and radiometric signal between Earth, Mars and the Moon with 100,000 points per body and 24 mission sites, at 0.05° worldwide and 30 arc-seconds for Ecuador and Galápagos. The evaluation included leave-one-mission-out tests, exact permutation, sensitivity to references, variables and thresholds, spatial autocorrelation and MODIS quality control. Nine Martian missions gave an AUC of 0.40 at both scales: the index does not separate high from medium hydrogeomorphic evidence. Quality control changed our first conclusions: of 17,236 eligible Ecuadorian cells, only 391 meet MODIS QA ≤ 1 and none of the high-similarity (≥95) cells pass; the two joint candidates had QA 3 and 5 and were withdrawn. We deliver global and Ecuador maps, an interactive web app with a 3D viewer, reproducible tables and an English technical article, and we state where the analogy breaks. It is a low-cost screening tool, not a probability of success or a station suitability score.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ANALOG-Δ ranks Earth's land surface by how closely its elevation, slope and radiometric signal match the surroundings of 24 real mission sites (10 Mars, 14 Moon). Each variable is converted to a percentile within its own body, so Earth, Moon and Mars are compared by relative position, not by physically incompatible absolute values. The result is a 0–100 similarity index, mapped worldwide and for Ecuador and Galápagos, and a set of statistical and quality tests that say how far those maps can be trusted.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Planetary data (NASA PDS): MGS MOLA MEGDR elevation and MGS TES bolometric albedo for Mars; LRO LOLA LDEM_64 elevation and LROC WAC 643 nm reflectance for the Moon.

2. Earth data: MODIS MCD43C3 v061 white-sky albedo (with its Albedo_Quality, Percent_Inputs and Percent_Snow layers), GMTED2010 elevation and slope, ESA CCI Land Cover 2022 mask.

3. 100,000 area-weighted random points per body define the percentile reference. Mission signatures are the median of a 9 × 9 grid (~1 km spacing) around each site. Martian references: Phoenix, Pathfinder, Perseverance, Opportunity and Curiosity; lunar references: all 14 sites.

4. Index = equal-weight Euclidean distance to the nearest signature, expressed as the share of the terrestrial background that is farther away. Joint index = minimum of Mars and Moon.

5. Two models: global at 0.05° (2,584,921 cells) and Ecuador at 30 arc-seconds (17,236 cells), with different support and masks.

EVALUATION AND QUALITY CONTROL — REPORTED EVEN WHEN IT FAILS

- Leave-one-mission-out with nine Martian missions (5 high vs 4 medium/medium-high), exact permutation over all 126 label assignments: AUC 0.40 globally (p = 0.683) and in Ecuador (p = 0.714). No useful discrimination.

- Sensitivity: removing Phoenix drops the area Jaccard of the ≥95 selection to 0.516; removing Opportunity gives 0.905. Weights, variables and thresholds also tested.

- Spatial autocorrelation in Ecuador (Moran's I 0.72–0.99, p = 0.005): cells are not independent observations.

- MODIS quality control: globally, QA ≤ 1 keeps 53.3% of the area. In Ecuador, only 391 of 17,236 cells meet QA ≤ 1 and no cell with similarity ≥95 survives, even with the permissive QA ≤ 2. The two joint candidates (QA 3 and 5) were withdrawn. Adding terrain and edge screening leaves 29 cells, none with high similarity.

- Conclusion: the radiometric data used are not good enough to prioritize Ecuadorian sites. This does not show that Ecuador lacks analogs; it shows what data are needed next.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Low-cost screening: open data and a laptop can rank the whole planet before anyone pays for a field campaign, and the quality tests show where a cheap screen is not enough.

- A method other teams can reuse: every candidate passes through validation and quality control before it is called an analog.

- Ecuador and Galápagos, rarely studied as analogs, combine young lava fields and high Andean volcanic plains within one small country. Our tests show they need better data (cloud-free albedo, mineralogy, thermal inertia) before field use.

- An interactive web app with three reading levels and a 3D viewer for students and the public.

WHERE THE ANALOGY BREAKS

Only three surface variables: no mineralogy, thermal inertia, radar, ice or climate. Albedo products differ physically between bodies, so comparison is ordinal. MODIS albedo keeps a ~5.6 km footprint. Earth cannot reproduce lunar (1.62 m/s²) or Martian (3.71 m/s²) gravity, the lunar vacuum, the thin Martian atmosphere or space radiation. No site is proposed for landing or a permanent station.

CREATIVITY

Instead of presenting a place that looks alien, we built a planet-wide screen and then tried hard to break it. The quality control overturned our own first candidates, and we publish that as a result.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, GeoPandas, rasterio, GDAL, pyhdf), QGIS 3.40, Google Earth Engine, Supabase/PostGIS, React + Vite + TypeScript, Unity 6 WebGL, Vercel, GitHub.

LINKS AND TEAM

Live app: https://devebug-analog-spaceapps.vercel.app/

Code (GPL-3.0): https://github.com/ronaldsoft/NASA-Space-Challange

Data, article and fact sheet: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1qXD29SfiK1VEmG0Q77ZhQHxE7okwt_T0

Team (Tena and Sangolquí, Ecuador): Ronald Rivera, Gabriel Criollo, Sofía Barros, Mateo Noboa, Yojar Lara, Sedney Vera.

AI USE

AI assistants (Claude, Grok Bot agents, OpenAI ChatGPT and Codex) helped write code, organize results and draft documentation. The team defined the method, ran and checked every result and reviewed all content. No data or figures were generated by AI. No NASA logos are used. Code with AI assistance · AI voice.
